units.title: C Foundation
units.tip: Objective-C is built on top of C, so understanding C basics is essential. You need to know variables, data types, functions, and control flow before learning Objective-C specific features.

exercises.question: What is the correct syntax to declare an integer variable named count in C?
exercises.answer: int count;
exercises.explain: In C, integer variables are declared with the int keyword followed by the variable name and a semicolon. This allocates memory for an integer value.

exercises.question: What does the char data type represent in C?
exercises.answer: A single character
exercises.explain: The char data type stores a single character, like 'A' or '5'. It occupies 1 byte of memory and can also hold small integer values.

exercises.question: What is the purpose of the float data type?
exercises.answer: To store decimal numbers with single precision
exercises.explain: The float type stores floating-point numbers (decimals) with 32-bit precision. For more precision, use double, which is 64-bit.
choices: To store decimal numbers with single precision

exercises.question: In C, what is the difference between float and double?
exercises.answer: double has more precision (64-bit vs 32-bit)
exercises.explain: Both float and double store decimal numbers, but double uses 64 bits for storage while float uses 32 bits. This makes double more precise for calculations.
choices: they are identical, just different names
float stores integers, double stores decimals
float is for functions, double is for variables

exercises.question: How do you declare a boolean value in C (before C99)?
exercises.answer: Use int with 0 for false and non-zero for true
exercises.explain: Early C did not have a built-in boolean type. Programmers used int values, where 0 means false and any non-zero value means true. C99 added the bool type.
choices: Use int with 0 for false and non-zero for true
C does not support boolean values

exercises.question: What does the unary & operator do in C?
exercises.answer: Returns the memory address of a variable
exercises.explain: The & operator is the address-of operator. It returns the memory address where a variable is stored, which can be assigned to a pointer.
choices: Returns the memory address of a variable

exercises.question: What does *ptr do in an expression, when ptr is a pointer?
exercises.answer: Dereferences a pointer to access its value
exercises.explain: The * operator dereferences a pointer, meaning it follows the address stored in the pointer to access the actual value at that location in memory.
choices: Takes the address of the pointer
Frees the memory the pointer refers to
Dereferences a pointer to access its value
Converts the pointer to an integer

exercises.question: What is the correct syntax to declare a pointer to an integer?
exercises.answer: int *ptr;
exercises.explain: A pointer to an integer is declared with int *ptr; The * indicates that ptr stores a memory address, not an integer value directly.

exercises.question: What is a NULL pointer?
exercises.answer: A pointer that does not point to any valid object
exercises.explain: A NULL pointer is a special pointer value that represents no valid address. It is used to indicate that a pointer does not currently refer to anything.
choices: A pointer that does not point to any valid object
A pointer to the beginning of memory

exercises.question: What does malloc() do in C?
exercises.answer: Allocates memory on the heap and returns a pointer
exercises.explain: malloc() (memory allocate) dynamically allocates a block of memory on the heap at runtime and returns a pointer to the start of that block.
choices: Allocates memory on the heap and returns a pointer

units.title: Objective-C Basics
units.tip: Objective-C adds object-oriented features to C. The main difference is message sending: instead of calling methods like functions, you send messages to objects using bracket syntax. This makes Objective-C very expressive and flexible.

exercises.question: What is the key difference between Objective-C and C?
exercises.answer: Objective-C adds object-oriented programming with message sending
exercises.explain: Objective-C is a superset of C that adds objects, classes, and a message-passing system. You send messages to objects rather than calling functions directly.
choices: Objective-C adds object-oriented programming with message sending

exercises.question: What is the correct syntax to send a message to an object in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: [object method];
exercises.explain: In Objective-C, you send messages using bracket syntax: [receiver message]. This is different from calling a function. The receiver is the object, and the message is the method.

exercises.question: How do you send a message with parameters in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: [object method:parameter];
exercises.explain: Messages with parameters use colons to separate the message parts. For one parameter: [object method:param]. Multiple parameters: [object method:p1 withValue:p2].

exercises.question: What is an object in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: An instance of a class that contains data and methods
exercises.explain: An object is a specific instance of a class. It has instance variables (data) and can receive messages (calls to methods). Objects are created from class definitions.
choices: A variable that stores a number
An instance of a class that contains data and methods
A function that performs a task

exercises.question: What does the alloc message do in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: Allocates memory for a new object
exercises.explain: The alloc message allocates memory on the heap for a new object instance. It is typically followed by init to initialize that object.
choices: Sends a message to all objects
Allocates memory for a new object

exercises.question: What is a class in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: A blueprint that defines the structure and behavior of objects
exercises.explain: A class is a template. It defines what instance variables objects will have and what methods they can respond to. Specific objects are instances of that class.
choices: A blueprint that defines the structure and behavior of objects

exercises.question: How do you create an instance of a class named Dog?
exercises.answer: Dog *myDog = [[Dog alloc] init];
exercises.explain: To create an instance, you send the alloc message to the class (allocating memory), then send init to that result (initializing it). The variable stores a pointer to the object.

exercises.question: What does the init message do?
exercises.answer: Initializes an object's instance variables to starting values
exercises.explain: The init method sets up an object after memory is allocated. It initializes instance variables and prepares the object for use.
choices: Initializes an object's instance variables to starting values
Sends a message to another object

exercises.question: In Objective-C, what is an instance variable?
exercises.answer: A variable that belongs to a specific object instance
exercises.explain: Each object has its own copy of instance variables (also called ivars). These variables store the object's state. For example, a Person object might have a name ivar.
choices: A variable declared in a function
A variable that belongs to a specific object instance
A variable that is shared by all objects of a class

exercises.question: What is a method in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: A function that belongs to a class and operates on objects of that class
exercises.explain: A method is similar to a function, but it is associated with a class. Methods can access and modify the instance variables of an object.
choices: A special pointer to a variable
A function that belongs to a class and operates on objects of that class

units.title: Classes and Methods
units.tip: Every Objective-C class has two parts: @interface declares what a class looks like (instance variables and method signatures), and @implementation defines what those methods do. Understanding this separation is key to reading and writing Objective-C code.

exercises.question: What does the @interface section declare in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: The class name, superclass, instance variables, and method signatures
exercises.explain: The @interface is the public contract of a class. It tells other code what methods are available and what instance variables the class has. It is usually placed in a header (.h) file.
choices: The class name, superclass, instance variables, and method signatures
Only messages that objects respond to

exercises.question: What is the correct syntax to declare a class Dog that inherits from NSObject?
exercises.answer: @interface Dog : NSObject { }
exercises.explain: A class declaration uses @interface ClassName : Superclass. NSObject is the base class for most Objective-C classes. Instance variables go between curly braces.

exercises.question: How do you declare a method signature in @interface?
exercises.answer: - (return_type)methodName:(parameter_type)param;
exercises.explain: Instance method signatures start with -, class methods with +. The return type goes in parentheses, followed by the method name and parameters in the format name:(type)param.

exercises.question: What do instance variables in @interface represent?
exercises.answer: Data stored in each object instance
exercises.explain: Instance variables (ivars) are declared between { } in the @interface. Each object of the class gets its own copy of these variables to hold its state.
choices: Functions that the class can call
Data stored in each object instance

exercises.question: What is the difference between @interface and @implementation?
exercises.answer: @interface declares what exists, @implementation defines how it works
exercises.explain: @interface is the specification (public contract), usually in a .h file. @implementation contains the actual code (method bodies), usually in a .m file.
choices: @interface declares what exists, @implementation defines how it works

exercises.question: What does the @implementation section contain in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: The actual code that defines what methods do
exercises.explain: The @implementation block contains the method implementations (the code inside each method). It corresponds to the method signatures declared in @interface.
choices: The actual code that defines what methods do

exercises.question: How do you implement a method in @implementation?
exercises.answer: - (return_type)methodName:(parameter_type)param { /* code */ }
exercises.explain: Method implementations match the signature from @interface, with the method body in curly braces. The syntax must match exactly.

exercises.question: What does the self keyword represent in an Objective-C method?
exercises.answer: A pointer to the current object instance
exercises.explain: self is an implicit parameter passed to every instance method. It refers to the object that received the message, so you use it to send messages to the object itself.
choices: A pointer to the current object instance

exercises.question: Inside a method, how do you directly access the instance variable that backs a property named age?
exercises.answer: _age or self->_age
exercises.explain: A property named age is backed by an instance variable named _age by default. You can reach it directly as _age or as self->_age. Writing self.age calls the getter or setter instead.

exercises.question: Which return type is preferred for an initializer like init in modern Objective-C?
exercises.answer: instancetype
exercises.explain: Initialization methods return instancetype, which means they return an instance of the class. This is better than returning id because it provides type safety.

units.title: Properties and Data
units.tip: Properties are a modern Objective-C feature that simplify working with instance variables. A property generates getter and setter methods automatically. Foundation classes like NSString, NSArray, and NSDictionary are essential for working with collections and strings in Objective-C.

exercises.question: What is a property in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: A synthesized getter/setter pair for an instance variable
exercises.explain: A property is declared in @interface and automatically generates getter and setter methods. Instead of writing methods manually, the compiler creates them for you.
choices: A method that accesses a variable
A synthesized getter/setter pair for an instance variable

exercises.question: How do you declare a property named name of type NSString?
exercises.answer: @property (nonatomic, strong) NSString *name;
exercises.explain: Properties are declared with @property, followed by attributes in parentheses (like nonatomic, strong), then the type and name. This creates automatic getter and setter methods.

exercises.question: What does the (nonatomic) attribute mean in a property?
exercises.answer: The property is not thread-safe, but faster
exercises.explain: nonatomic means the getter and setter are not protected for multi-threaded access. This is faster but less safe if multiple threads access the property.
choices: The property is not thread-safe, but faster
The property must be a whole number
The property is stored in an array

exercises.question: What does the (strong) attribute mean in a property?
exercises.answer: The object's reference count is incremented when assigned
exercises.explain: strong means the property holds a strong reference to the object. The reference count increases when assigned, preventing the object from being deallocated.
choices: The object's reference count is incremented when assigned
The property is the main property

exercises.question: What does the (weak) attribute mean in a property?
exercises.answer: The property does not prevent the object from being deallocated
exercises.explain: weak means the property does not increment the reference count. If the referenced object is deallocated, the weak property automatically becomes nil.
choices: The property has weaker access control
The property does not prevent the object from being deallocated
The property must be checked before use

exercises.question: What is NSString in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: An immutable class for storing text strings
exercises.explain: NSString is a Foundation class that represents text. NSString objects are immutable (cannot be changed). NSMutableString is the mutable version for strings that can be modified.
choices: An immutable class for storing text strings

exercises.question: How do you create an NSString with a literal in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: NSString *str = @"Hello";
exercises.explain: String literals in Objective-C are created with the @ symbol. @"Hello" creates an NSString object. This is the preferred way to create string literals.

exercises.question: What is NSArray in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: An immutable class that stores an ordered collection of objects
exercises.explain: NSArray is a Foundation class for storing collections of objects in order. NSArray is immutable. NSMutableArray is the mutable version for collections that can change.
choices: An immutable class that stores an ordered collection of objects

exercises.question: What is NSDictionary in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: An immutable class that stores key-value pairs
exercises.explain: NSDictionary is a Foundation class for storing pairs of keys and values. Like NSArray, it is immutable. NSMutableDictionary is mutable.
choices: An immutable class that stores key-value pairs

exercises.question: Using message syntax, how do you access the element at index 0 in an NSArray named array?
exercises.answer: [array objectAtIndex:0];
exercises.explain: NSArray elements are accessed with the objectAtIndex: message. In modern Objective-C, you can also use subscript syntax: array[0].

units.title: Memory Management
units.tip: Memory management is critical in Objective-C. The language uses reference counting to track when objects should be deallocated. Modern Objective-C uses ARC (Automatic Reference Counting), which automatically manages reference counts. Understanding both helps you write safe, efficient code.

exercises.question: What is reference counting in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: A system that tracks how many pointers reference an object
exercises.explain: Each Objective-C object has a reference count. When you create a strong reference to an object, its count increases. When references are removed, the count decreases.
choices: A system that tracks how many pointers reference an object
A way to count how many objects exist
A limit on the number of objects

exercises.question: What does the retain message do in manual memory management?
exercises.answer: Increments the object's reference count
exercises.explain: retain increments the reference count, indicating another owner has a reference. The paired release decrements it. When the count reaches zero, the object is deallocated.

exercises.question: What does the release message do in manual memory management?
exercises.answer: Decrements the object's reference count
exercises.explain: release decrements the reference count. If the count reaches zero, the object is deallocated and its dealloc method is called.
choices: Sends a message to the object

exercises.question: When does an object get deallocated in reference counting?
exercises.answer: When its reference count reaches zero
exercises.explain: Objects are deallocated when the reference count drops to zero. This means all owners have released their references, and the object is no longer needed.
choices: When it is no longer visible in code
When its reference count reaches zero

exercises.question: What is a retain cycle (or circular reference)?
exercises.answer: When two objects hold strong references to each other, preventing deallocation
exercises.explain: If object A holds a strong reference to object B, and B holds a strong reference to A, neither can be deallocated. Using weak references breaks the cycle.
choices: When two objects hold strong references to each other, preventing deallocation
A normal part of object initialization

exercises.question: What does ARC stand for in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: Automatic Reference Counting
exercises.explain: ARC is a compiler feature that automatically manages reference counts. Instead of manually sending retain and release, the compiler inserts them for you.

exercises.question: How does ARC differ from manual reference counting?
exercises.answer: ARC automatically inserts retain/release calls at compile time
exercises.explain: With ARC, you write code without retain/release calls. The compiler analyzes the code and automatically inserts memory management calls where needed.
choices: ARC is slower than manual management
ARC automatically inserts retain/release calls at compile time

exercises.question: In ARC, what is a strong reference?
exercises.answer: A reference that keeps an object in memory
exercises.explain: A strong reference (the default in ARC) increments the reference count and prevents the object from being deallocated as long as the reference exists.
choices: A reference that can only be used once
A reference that points to another reference
A reference that keeps an object in memory

exercises.question: In ARC, how do you declare a weak local variable?
exercises.answer: __weak MyClass *ref;
exercises.explain: The __weak qualifier declares a weak reference. In a property, use the (weak) attribute instead. Weak references do not prevent deallocation and automatically become nil when the object is deallocated.

exercises.question: When should you use a weak reference in ARC?
exercises.answer: To avoid retain cycles in parent-child relationships
exercises.explain: Weak references break retain cycles. If a parent object owns a child, the child should use a weak reference back to the parent to prevent them from keeping each other alive.
choices: To avoid retain cycles in parent-child relationships
When you want to save memory

units.title: Advanced OOP
units.tip: Protocols define a contract of methods that a class must implement. Categories allow you to add new methods to existing classes. Both features make Objective-C code flexible and reusable, essential for building maintainable Apple applications.

exercises.question: What is a protocol in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: A declared set of methods that adopting classes implement
exercises.explain: A protocol defines a contract. A class that adopts a protocol must implement its required methods, and may implement its optional ones. Similar to interfaces in other languages.
choices: A way to inherit from multiple classes
A method that communicates between objects
A declared set of methods that adopting classes implement

exercises.question: How do you declare a protocol in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: @protocol ProtocolName <NSObject> ... @end
exercises.explain: Protocols are declared with @protocol ProtocolName, often inheriting from NSObject. Method signatures are listed inside, followed by @end.

exercises.question: How does a class adopt a protocol in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: @interface ClassName <ProtocolName> ... @end
exercises.explain: A class adopts a protocol by listing it in angle brackets after the superclass in @interface. The class must then implement all required methods from the protocol.

exercises.question: What is an optional method in a protocol?
exercises.answer: A method a class may implement but is not required to
exercises.explain: Methods marked with @optional in a protocol are optional; classes that adopt the protocol do not have to implement them. @required marks methods that must be implemented.
choices: A method that appears once per program
A method a class may implement but is not required to
A method that takes no parameters

exercises.question: Why are protocols useful in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: They define contracts and enable flexible polymorphic code
exercises.explain: Protocols let you specify required functionality without caring about the concrete class. You can write code that works with any object that implements a protocol.
choices: They define contracts and enable flexible polymorphic code
They are only for memory management

exercises.question: What is a category in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: A way to add methods to an existing class without subclassing
exercises.explain: Categories extend existing classes by adding new methods. You can add methods to NSString, NSArray, or any class, even if you don't have the source code.
choices: A way to add methods to an existing class without subclassing

exercises.question: How do you declare a category in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: @interface ClassName (CategoryName) ... @end
exercises.explain: Categories are declared with @interface ClassName (CategoryName). The category name goes in parentheses. Methods are listed inside just like @interface.

exercises.question: Can categories add instance variables to a class?
exercises.answer: No, categories cannot add instance variables
exercises.explain: Categories cannot add stored instance variables. To add them, you must subclass the class or use a class extension in the class's own source.
choices: No, categories cannot add instance variables

exercises.question: What is a class extension in Objective-C?
exercises.answer: An unnamed category used for private methods and properties
exercises.explain: A class extension is written as @interface ClassName () ... @end (no name in parentheses). It is typically in the .m file and used for private implementation details.
choices: An unnamed category used for private methods and properties

exercises.question: What is the difference between a category and subclassing?
exercises.answer: Categories add methods to existing classes; subclassing creates a new class hierarchy
exercises.explain: Categories modify existing classes globally. Subclassing creates a new class that inherits from another. Use categories for convenience methods; use subclassing when you need new ivars or to override behavior selectively.
choices: Categories add methods to existing classes; subclassing creates a new class hierarchy
